title: The Ring
summary: Tilewise caches map tiles on three servers. Adding a fourth with hash % N would wipe out three quarters of the cache. Consistent hashing puts servers and keys on a ring so only a small slice moves.

goals.text: See why hash % N reshuffles almost every key when N changes
Place servers and keys on a hash ring and find a key's owner
Show that adding or removing a server moves only ~1/N of keys
Use virtual nodes to balance load

steps.title: Three caches and a simple rule
body: Tilewise serves map tiles. Rendering a tile takes ~120 ms, so rendered tiles are kept in a fleet of cache servers; 92% of requests are hits.
To pick a cache, every API node computes hash(tile_id) % 3. Same tile, same answer, on every node — no lookup table needed, and tiles spread evenly.

card.title: Which cache holds a tile?
lines: cache = hash(tile_id) % 3
= every API node computes the same answer
= no lookup table, keys spread evenly

steps.title: Adding a server reshuffles everything
body: Traffic grows, so the team adds cache D and switches to % 4. A tile keeps its server only if its hash leaves the same remainder for 3 and for 4 — true for about 1 in 4 tiles.
So ~75% of tiles are suddenly looked up on a server that doesn't have them. The hit rate collapses from 92% to about 25%, and the renderer is hit with four times its usual load.

callout.text: The same happens when a server dies: N drops by one and almost every key moves. A single failure becomes a fleet-wide cache flush.

card.title: hash % 3  vs  hash % 4
lines: ! a key stays only if both remainders match
! ≈ 1 in 4 stay → 75% of keys move at once

steps.title: Bend the hash space into a ring
body: Consistent hashing hashes servers as well as keys into the same range (say 0 to 2³²−1) and bends that range into a circle, so the largest value sits next to 0.
Each server owns the stretch of ring between its point and the next server's point. To find a tile, hash it to a point and see whose stretch it falls in. The rule involves no N at all.
changes: + Hash ring with servers A, B, C

card.title: Put servers and keys on a circle
lines: hash space 0 … 2³² − 1, bent into a ring
each server hashed to a point (◆)
each key hashed to a point (●)
= a key belongs to the server whose stretch it lands in
# arc colour = owning server

steps.title: A new server takes one slice
body: Now add cache D. It hashes to a point inside B's stretch and takes over just the part between its point and the next server. Every other key keeps its owner.

In the picture, 6 of 24 keys move (25% of keys). In general a new server takes about 1/N of the keys — the minimum possible, since it has to hold its share of something. The hit rate dips to ~70% and refills quickly.
changes: ~ Keys in B's old slice now belong to D

card.title: Adding cache D
lines: D lands in the middle of B's stretch
only keys in that slice change owner (circled)
= 6 of 24 keys moved; A and C untouched
# on average a new server takes ~1/N of the keys

steps.title: Random points make lumpy shares
body: With one point per server, stretch sizes are left to chance. Here cache A owns 36% of the ring and cache C only 14% — A runs hot while C idles.
Failures are lumpy too: when a server dies, its whole stretch lands on a single neighbour, which may then tip over as well.

card.title: Share of the ring
lines: # one random point per server → lumpy stretches

steps.title: Many small points per server
body: Give each server many points on the ring — virtual nodes — by hashing "cache-A#1", "cache-A#2", and so on. Each server now owns many small stretches scattered around the circle.
With 100–256 virtual nodes each, shares average out to within a few percent. A more powerful server can simply get more virtual nodes.
changes: ~ Each server placed at several points on the ring

card.title: Share with 128 virtual nodes each
lines: # ring shows 3 per server; real setups use 100–256

steps.title: Losing a server moves only its keys
body: Cache B crashes. Its points leave the ring and each of its small stretches falls to whichever server comes next — sometimes A, sometimes C, sometimes D.
Only B's keys move (5 of 24 here), and the extra load is shared by all survivors instead of crushing one neighbour.
changes: ~ B's keys spread over A, C and D

card.title: Cache B fails
lines: B's points vanish from the ring
each of its stretches falls to the next server along
= 5 of 24 keys moved — only B's
= spread over A, C and D, not dumped on one neighbour

steps.title: Where the ring shows up
body: Distributed databases use the same ring to place data: a key lives on its owner and is replicated to the next few distinct servers along the ring, so a failure already has copies nearby.
The trade-offs: every client must share the same server list and hash function, and a single very hot key still lands on one server — the ring balances keys, not traffic per key.

callout.text: Many systems use fixed hash partitions plus a lookup map instead (as in the previous lesson). Both aim at the same goal: grow without moving everything.

changes: + Replicas on the next servers along the ring

card.title: Beyond caches
lines: replicas: keep a key on its owner plus the next
2 distinct servers along the ring
used by distributed key-value and wide-column stores,
client-side cache sharding, and some load balancers
# weight a bigger server by giving it more virtual nodes

steps.title: Consistent hashing in one breath
body:
• hash % N is simple but moves almost every key when N changes.
  • On a hash ring, servers and keys share one circle; a key belongs to the stretch it lands in.
  • Adding or removing a server moves only ~1/N of the keys.
  • Virtual nodes balance shares and spread a failed server's load across all survivors.

card.title: Consistent hashing
lines: ! hash % N: changing N moves almost every key
ring: a new server takes only its slice, ~1/N
virtual nodes even out shares and failures
= any client computes the owner — no central lookup
